content: Environmental degradation refers to the progressive deterioration of the environment caused by the depletion of essential resources such as air, water, and soil. It also encompasses the destruction of ecosystems and the extinction of wildlife species. This phenomenon has been identified as one of the ten critical threats officially recognized by the High-Level Threat Panel of the United Nations. On May 1, 1998, a significant report addressing global health and environmental issues was jointly released by the World Resources Institute (WRI), the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), and the World Bank. This report, titled Environmental Change and Human Health, was a special section of World Resources 1998-99. It highlighted the alarming prevalence of preventable illnesses and premature deaths occurring on a massive scale worldwide. The report emphasized that substantial improvements in human health could lead to millions of people living longer and healthier lives than ever before. However, in the poorest regions of the world, approximately one in five children does not survive to their fifth birthday, primarily due to diseases linked to environmental factors. Globally, an estimated 11 million children die each year, a number equivalent to the combined populations of Norway and Switzerland. The majority of these deaths are attributed to preventable illnesses such as malaria, acute respiratory infections, and diarrheal diseases.
